scenes.narration: By the time Lynden Pindling reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Sir Lynden Oscar Pindling, (22 March 1930 – 26 August 2000) was a Bahamian politician who was the first prime minister of the Bahamas from 1973 to 1992. Pindling is regarded by some as the "Father of the Nation", having led the Bahamas to majority rule and independence.

The rise of Lynden Pindling was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. Pindling served as the first black colonial premier of the Bahamas from 1967 to 1969, being the second and final officeholder. He was leader of the Progressive Liberal Party (PLP) from 1956 to 1997 when he resigned from public life under scandal.

Setbacks came early for Lynden Pindling, and the response to them is the real story. Pindling won an unbroken string of general elections until 1992, when the PLP lost to the Free National Movement (FNM) led by Hubert Alexander Ingraham. He conceded defeat with the words: "the people of this great little democracy have spoken in a most dignified and eloquent manner and the voice of the people, is the voice of God".

The legacy of Lynden Pindling outlived the circumstances that produced it. Pindling was born on 22 March 1930 to Arnold and Viola (née Bain) Pindling in his grandfather's home in Mason's Addition, Nassau. Pindling's father was a native of Jamaica who had immigrated to the Bahamas to join the Royal Bahamas Police Force as a constable.

Few lives travel as far as that of Lynden Pindling, and the distance is the point. Pindling's mother hailed from the island of Acklins, which she left as a child. As a young boy, Pindling worked for his father's small grocery store which was attached to their home in East Street.

The childhood of Lynden Pindling contains the adult in small print. He became chief delivery boy using the handlebars of his bike to make drop-offs in neighbouring areas. Pindling's parents wanted the best possible education available to him that they could afford, which led to Pindling transferring schools frequently in his earlier years.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Lynden Pindling — in that order. He first attended Eastern Primary School, then located on School Lane between Shirley and Dowdeswell Street. Between the ages seven and nine, Pindling attended all three of the government's junior schools.

The turning point in the life of Lynden Pindling looked like a failure at the time. He spent approximately one year each at Eastern Junior on Bay Street, Southern Junior on Wulff Road and Western Junior on the corner of Meeting Street and Hospital Lane. He then spent three years at Western Senior School from 1940 to 1943, where the head teacher was musician (and composer of the Bahamian National anthem), Timothy Gibson from whom Pindling also later took piano lessons.

Every biography of Lynden Pindling has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. In the summer of 1943, Pindling along with hundreds of children from all over The Bahamas took examinations for enrolment in the selective Government High School (GHS). Pindling went on to study at King's College, University of London (1948–52), from which he received a law degree.

The education of Lynden Pindling happened mostly outside any school. He was admitted to the Middle Temple on 12 October 1948 and was Called to the Bar on 10 February 1953. The following month, he successfully contested Nassau's Southern District constituency in the 1956 general election.

What Lynden Pindling wanted at the start and what Lynden Pindling got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. He became Parliamentary Leader of the party when PLP Chairman and de facto leader, Henry Taylor, was defeated in the 1956 general election. Pindling was elected the party's Parliamentary Leader over the dynamic and popular labour leader Randol Fawkes.

The defining trait of Lynden Pindling was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. He would go on to win successive elections to the House of Assembly in 1962, 1967, 1968, 1972, 1977, 1982, 1987, 1992 and 1997. On 27 April 1965, a day known in Bahamian history as "Black Tuesday", Pindling delivered a speech in the House of Assembly.

Those who met Lynden Pindling at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. In a dramatic turn of events, Pindling ended his speech by taking the Speaker's Mace and, in a dramatic power-to-the-people gesture, throwing the mace out of a window onto the street, which temporarily halted proceedings. Pindling was elected in 1967 on a platform that included hostility to gambling, corruption and the Bay Street Boys' mob connections.

The private years of Lynden Pindling explain the public decades better than any speech. On 10 January 1967, the PLP and the governing United Bahamian Party (led by Sir Roland Symonette) each won 18 seats in the Assembly. Randol Fawkes, the lone Labour MP, and Alvin Braynen, lent their votes to PLP allowing Pindling to form the first black government in Bahamian history.

The family Lynden Pindling came from matters more than the legends admit. He introduced social security measures in the form of the National Insurance Scheme, and the formation of the College of The Bahamas and the Royal Bahamas Defence Force. In 1966–67, the British government sent a Royal Commission of Inquiry to Nassau to investigate charges of widespread corruption in the Bahamian political system.

The first real success of Lynden Pindling arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. The four-man commission was headed by Sir Ranulph Bacon, who had recently retired as deputy commander of Scotland Yard. The commission also found, however, that Pindling, during his campaign, had been funded and aided by U.S. casino operator Michael McLaney in the expectation that Pindling would permit McLaney to operate in the islands.

The last chapter of Lynden Pindling was written long after the fame. Because of the report, Pindling broke his link with McLaney but was not himself prosecuted. Certain prominent mob figures, including Dino Cellini, were exiled from Bahamas but casino operations continued.

The whole life of Lynden Pindling reads like a single decision repeated. Pindling told the commission that U.S. interests had first approached him with evidence to implicate the UBP in corruption, which led to the royal commission. Senate subcommittee investigation of corrupt offshore finances, mob elements accused Mike McLaney and his associate Elliott Roosevelt of having offered a contract to kill Pindling for reneging on the deal.

Between the birth and the legend of Lynden Pindling lie the years that actually decide it. This plot was discredited, but new elements of the control of the Miami Beach-based, Meyer Lansky-led syndicate over Bahamian business and politics emerged, as well as details of McLaney's dealings with Pindling, which included cash, aircraft, boats, and a campaign headquarters on Bay Street. In 1983, a report entitled The Bahamas: A Nation For Sale by investigative television journalist Brian Ross was aired on NBC in the United States.

The reputation of Lynden Pindling was built in the middle, not at the edges. The report claimed Pindling and his government accepted bribes from Colombian drug smugglers, particularly the notorious Carlos Lehder, co-founder of the Medellín Cartel, in exchange for allowing the smugglers to use the Bahamas as a transshipment point to smuggle Colombian cocaine into the US. Through murder and extortion, Lehder had gained complete control over the Norman's Cay in Exuma, which became the chief base for smuggling cocaine into the United States.

Somebody like Lynden Pindling should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. The public outcry, however, led to the creation in 1983 of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Drug Trafficking and Government Corruption in the Bahamas. A review of Pindling's personal finances by the Commission found that he had spent eight times his reported earnings from 1977 to 1984.

The life of Lynden Pindling begins far from where the story usually starts. The commission eventually cleared Sir Lynden of any wrongdoing, but said that he and his wife had at least $3.5 million in bank deposits that could not be accounted for. Pindling was able to win reelection in 1987 by focusing on nationalist and racial appeals as ways to combat the drug and corruption charges.

Lynden Pindling was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. However, in August 1992, the opposition Free National Movement (FNM) defeated the PLP in the general election due in part to scandals about the state-owned airline and the Bahamas Hotel Corporation run by the Pindlings. The FNM would go on to win a second landslide victory in 1997, and Pindling retired from politics shortly afterward.

To understand where Lynden Pindling ended up, start with where Lynden Pindling began. On 5 May 1956, Pindling married Marguerite McKenzie (later Lady Pindling and, in her own right, Dame Marguerite Pindling), of Long Bay Cays in Andros, at St Ann's Parish on Fox Hill Road in Nassau. Pindling was sworn in as a member of Her Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council (PC) in 1976, and he was appointed Knight Commander of the Order of St.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Lynden Pindling ran through years nobody filmed. In early 1996, Pindling began showing signs of tiredness and was diagnosed with early stage prostate cancer. He underwent a ten-week course of radiation treatment at Johns Hopkins Hospital's Oncology Center in Baltimore, and was given a clean bill of health, after which he returned to his post-Prime Minister work as lawyer.

Each stage of the life of Lynden Pindling made the next stage possible. Pindling died on Saturday, 26 August 2000 at his home on Skyline Drive, New Providence, surrounded by family. On 29 August, Parliament met, and then Prime Minister Hubert Ingraham and others paid public tribute.

The people who knew Lynden Pindling young describe someone already restless. Two days later, all members of the Bahamas Bar did the same in a special session of the Supreme Court. Pindling's body was displayed in the House of Assembly on Rawson Square, for public viewing for four days, beginning early in the morning on Thursday, 31 August.

What Lynden Pindling built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. On 4 September, a full state funeral was held at the Church of God of Prophecy in New Providence, led by a long procession, with the Royal Bahamas Police Force Band at its front and the Royal Bahamas Defence Force Band at its rear. In 2006, Nassau International Airport was renamed Lynden Pindling International Airport in his honour.
